summary:
SkyShift Observatory is an interactive astronomical research platform developed by Team Sagittarius A for NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. It transforms publicly available telescope observations into an accessible environment for investigating changes in the night sky.

Our platform integrates NASA's SPHEREx observations with complementary astronomical datasets from ZTF, Pan-STARRS, 2MASS, WISE, and Gaia. Users can search celestial coordinates, explore observations across different dates and wavelengths, compare images using blinking, overlays, and difference views, and investigate potential changes through coordinate alignment, exploratory motion analysis, catalog searches, and provenance-backed scientific reports.

SkyShift addresses the challenge by providing tools to examine how celestial objects appear or move across multiple observations—an essential step in investigating distant, previously unidentified Solar System objects such as the hypothetical Planet X.

Importantly, SkyShift distinguishes preliminary candidates from verified discoveries, highlighting measurement limitations, instrumental artifacts, and scientific uncertainty rather than presenting unvalidated detections as facts.

By combining astronomical data access, scientific investigation, and an intuitive interface, SkyShift aims to make the search for hidden celestial objects more transparent, reproducible, and accessible to students, researchers, and citizen scientists.
details:
SkyShift Observatory — Project Details

What We Developed

SkyShift Observatory is an interactive, web-based astronomical investigation platform developed by Team Sagittarius A for NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Its purpose is to make real astronomical observations accessible, comparable, and scientifically interpretable, helping researchers, students, and citizen scientists investigate changes in the night sky.

The search for a hypothetical distant Solar System planet requires examining faint astronomical objects across multiple observations. However, changes between telescope images can arise from genuine celestial motion, different observation wavelengths, instrumental characteristics, background noise, or image-processing artifacts.

SkyShift addresses this problem by bringing multiple astronomical archives, visualization tools, and exploratory scientific analysis into one integrated environment.

How It Works

The platform is organized into five main scientific workflows: Explore, Compare, Investigate, Reports, and Learn, alongside a dedicated IRSA Data Access Hub.

Explore: Users select celestial coordinates, observation dates, and wavelength ranges to search available astronomical data. SkyShift integrates NASA's SPHEREx observations with complementary information from ZTF, Pan-STARRS, Gaia, 2MASS, AllWISE, and Spitzer GLIMPSE. These integrations support different functions, including image retrieval, catalog queries, and positional investigation.

Compare: Users examine astronomical images through side-by-side views, blinking, overlays, and interactive comparison controls. World Coordinate System (WCS) information supports image alignment where appropriate. Native-pixel and smooth-display options improve visual inspection without inventing astronomical resolution. Diagnostic image differences are restricted to scientifically compatible observations.

Investigate: Users inspect image metadata, native FITS pixels, spectral intensity, uncertainties, and quality flags. The application supports human-guided candidate screening, preliminary multi-epoch motion analysis, and contextual checks against existing astronomical catalogs. These features are exploratory and do not constitute validated automatic object detection.

Reports: The platform produces downloadable scientific records containing observation information, analysis results, provenance, source hashes, and scientific limitations. This helps users preserve and review the evidence supporting their investigations.

Learn: Educational explanations introduce astronomical concepts such as parallax, wavelength-dependent observations, instrumental effects, and uncertainty, making the platform useful for learners as well as experienced investigators.

The IRSA Data Access Hub additionally provides access to 32 official astronomical resources. We implemented genuine native-resolution 2MASS FITS retrieval and verified catalog searches against 2MASS, AllWISE, and Spitzer GLIMPSE using official NASA/IPAC IRSA services.

Technology and Development

Our technical stack includes:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic.
  • Scientific computing: Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, FITS processing, WCS transformations, and astronomical image analysis.
  • Data access: NASA/IPAC IRSA archive interfaces, including SIA, TAP, and Gator, alongside selected external astronomical survey services.
  • Testing: Pytest, Playwright, and automated frontend build and validation tools.
  • Infrastructure: A locally hosted scientific backend, authenticated API access, Git version control, and temporary HTTPS deployment through Cloudflare Tunnel.

Development and testing were performed using our team's computers and publicly accessible astronomical datasets. No specialized telescope hardware was required.

AI-assisted tools, including ChatGPT, supported software development, debugging, testing, documentation, and interface development. Scientific interpretations remain subject to validation rather than being accepted solely because an AI system produces them.

Creativity and Innovation

SkyShift's central innovation is its combination of astronomical exploration with scientific transparency.

Rather than simply highlighting differences between images and claiming discoveries, the platform encourages users to investigate why those differences appear.

It combines multi-survey data access, interactive image comparison, spectral investigation, human-reviewed candidates, exploratory motion fitting, and evidence-based reporting in a single interface.

A distinctive feature is the separation of visual observations from scientific conclusions. SkyShift explicitly communicates when measurements are preliminary, when observations cannot be directly compared, and when an apparent change may result from instrumental effects.

This makes the platform not only a visualization tool but also an educational framework for responsible astronomical investigation.

Scientific Considerations and Challenges

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Differences in telescope resolution, wavelength coverage, observation dates, and measurement units.
  • Coordinate alignment, image masks, noise, point-spread functions, and instrumental artifacts.
  • The possibility of false positives when comparing images or identifying moving objects.
  • The importance of preserving original scientific data and documenting archive provenance.
  • Data-access limitations, API availability, processing performance, and application reliability.
  • Accessibility for students and citizen scientists without sacrificing scientific accuracy.

Our exploratory candidate markers and motion models are not calibrated Planet X detections or validated orbital solutions. Further scientific validation would require independent source association, improved photometric calibration, uncertainty propagation, and false-positive testing.

Benefits and Intended Impact

SkyShift Observatory aims to reduce the technical barriers separating the public from real astronomical research.

For students, it offers hands-on learning using authentic telescope data. For citizen scientists, it creates a structured environment for examining unusual astronomical observations. For researchers, it demonstrates an extensible approach to exploring multiple surveys while retaining evidence and scientific limitations.

Our long-term vision is to support transparent, reproducible investigations of changing and potentially unidentified celestial objects, including those relevant to the search for Planet X.

SkyShift Observatory does not claim to have discovered Planet X. Instead, it provides tools that help people explore the evidence, question apparent changes, and understand what would be required to establish a genuine astronomical discovery.
